title: One in Seven People Now Uses an AI Chatbot Instead of Seeing a Doctor. The Risks Are Not What You Expect.
excerpt: A major UK study finds 15 per cent of the public has replaced GP visits with AI, while a separate trial shows chatbots matching physicians on diagnosis. For a diaspora facing three-month specialist waits, the implications are personal.
body:
Fifteen per cent of the British public has now used an AI chatbot instead of contacting a GP or NHS service for a health concern, according to a major new study by King's Health Partners, Responsible AI UK, and The Policy Institute. A further 10 per cent have used AI for mental health or wellbeing support in place of a trained professional. The numbers are striking, but the detail buried inside them is what should concern anyone reaching for ChatGPT before reaching for the phone.

Among those who sought health advice from AI, up to 20 per cent reported that the chatbot did not encourage them to seek a professional opinion. A similar proportion decided against seeing a doctor entirely because of what the AI told them. In a system where early detection of conditions like cancer, diabetes, and heart disease is the single greatest predictor of survival, a chatbot that reassures when it should refer is not a convenience. It is a liability.

The Accuracy Paradox

The complication is that AI is genuinely getting better at diagnosis. An April 2026 study published in The New England Journal of Medicine found that OpenAI's o1 model achieved 78 per cent accuracy on complex diagnostic cases and outperformed experienced emergency room physicians on actual patient encounters. Google's AMIE chatbot, tested on real patients before their physician appointments, placed the correct diagnosis in its top three suggestions 75 per cent of the time.

These numbers sound reassuring until you understand what they leave out. As Dr Steven Rougas, who studies clinical decision-making at Brown University, has written: making the correct diagnosis is only half a doctor's job. The other half — management reasoning — involves deciding what to do about it, weighing competing treatments, factoring in a patient's other conditions, medications, social circumstances, and risk tolerance. On this dimension, human clinicians still outperform AI substantially. The AMIE trial noted that treatment plans proposed by human physicians were more practical and cost-effective than those proposed by the chatbot.

Why This Hits the Diaspora Differently

For South Asians living in the United States, United Kingdom, and Canada, the appeal of AI health advice is not hard to understand. In the UK, GP waiting times have stretched to weeks. In the US, seeing a specialist without a referral often means a three-month wait and a $300 consultation fee. In Canada, emergency room waits routinely exceed eight hours.

Add cultural factors: a reluctance in many South Asian families to discuss health concerns openly, a tradition of managing symptoms at home before escalating, and a generation of older parents who distrust Western medical systems. AI slots neatly into this gap. It is available at 2 AM. It does not judge. It speaks every language. And it gives you an answer in seconds.

The problem is that the answer may be confidently wrong in ways that are invisible to someone without medical training. AI excels at pattern matching: your symptoms match this condition with 87 per cent probability. What it cannot do is notice the subtle asymmetry in how you describe your pain, catch the hesitation that suggests you are minimising symptoms, or recognise that your family history of cardiac disease makes a seemingly minor complaint worth investigating immediately.

The South Asian Health Gap

South Asians already face disproportionate risks for cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, and metabolic syndrome. These are conditions where early, nuanced medical intervention matters enormously and where delays or missed signals can be catastrophic. If 15 per cent of the general population is substituting AI for professional care, the figure among technology-comfortable, wait-averse diaspora communities is likely higher.

Professor Graham Lord, Executive Director of King's Health Partners, put it directly: "When something goes wrong with AI, responsibility is often placed on clinicians, even where they have limited control over how AI tools are introduced. To realise AI's potential, we need greater transparency about what works, what is safe, how decisions are made, and how issues are handled."

The Right Way to Use AI for Health

None of this means AI has no role in healthcare. Used correctly, it can accelerate triage, help patients prepare better questions for their doctors, flag drug interactions, and provide health literacy at scale. The danger is not AI itself but the substitution — replacing professional judgement with algorithmic confidence, particularly for conditions that require context, nuance, and the kind of clinical intuition that comes from examining thousands of patients, not millions of data points.

If you are using ChatGPT or a similar tool for health advice, treat its output the way you would treat a well-informed friend's opinion: worth hearing, but never a substitute for a qualified assessment. And if the chatbot tells you not to worry, consider that the most dangerous medical advice is often the most reassuring.

Sources: King's Health Partners and The Policy Institute (2026); The New England Journal of Medicine (April 2026); Nature Medicine (2026); Fast Company (June 2026)
